nameStory: Toothed Streak-moss gets its name from the distinctive 'teeth' around the opening of its spore capsules and the streaked appearance of its leaf arrangement. When you look closely at this tiny moss, the leaves seem to form subtle streaks or lines as they spiral around the stem, creating a pattern that catches the eye of moss enthusiasts.
description: Toothed Streak-moss is a small, inconspicuous moss that forms loose tufts or scattered patches on rock surfaces. This diminutive plant rarely grows taller than half an inch, making it easy to overlook unless you're specifically searching for mosses. Its slender stems are topped with narrow, pointed leaves that curve and twist when dry, giving the whole plant a somewhat scraggly appearance. Like most mosses, it lacks flowers and reproduces through spores released from tiny capsules.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, loose tufts or scattered individual plants rather than dense mats, never more than about 12mm tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that curl and crisp when dry, becoming more erect when moist - they feel brittle to gentle touch

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Tiny oval capsules on short stalks with distinctive teeth around the opening, visible with a hand lens

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on acidic rock surfaces, especially granite and sandstone, never on soil or bark

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dull green when moist, becoming brownish or grayish-green when dry, blending in with rock surfaces

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and crispy when dry, becoming softer and more pliable within minutes of getting wet

habitat: This specialized moss is found exclusively on exposed acidic rock surfaces, particularly granite outcrops, cliff faces, and large boulders in forested areas. It prefers partially shaded locations where rocks stay somewhat moist but aren't constantly wet. In New England, look for it on the many granite formations throughout the region, especially in areas with clean air away from heavy pollution.

seasonality.spring: Most visible as it greens up with spring rains, leaves unfurl and become more recognizable. Sporophytes begin developing during wet periods.
seasonality.summer: Often appears dried and brownish during hot, dry spells but quickly revives with rain. Mature sporophytes may be present and releasing spores.
seasonality.fall: Becomes more noticeable as deciduous leaves fall away from rock surfaces. Fall rains bring out the green coloration again.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often dormant-looking and brown. Snow cover can keep it hydrated and occasionally green during warm spells.

funFact: Toothed Streak-moss can survive being completely dried out for months, losing up to 95% of its water content, then spring back to life within 20 minutes of getting wet - a superpower that allows it to thrive on bare rock where other plants would quickly die!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small rock-dwelling mosses, but its exclusive preference for acidic rock (never soil or bark) and the distinctive way its leaves curl up when dry help distinguish it. Remember: if it's not on rock, it's not Toothed Streak-moss.
contextualKnowledge: This moss is extremely rare in New England with only one confirmed observation, making any sighting potentially significant for scientific records. Its rarity may be due to air pollution sensitivity or very specific habitat requirements that are uncommon in the region.
compareHints: Since this is the only Rhabdoweisia species recorded in New England, compare it to other small rock mosses like Grimmia species. Unlike Grimmias which often form dense cushions, Toothed Streak-moss grows in looser tufts and has leaves that are less tightly curled when dry. The sporophyte teeth are also distinctively different when examined closely with magnification.
